general_rules: Two tasks; both must be completed. Task 2 contributes twice as much as Task 1 to the Writing band.
Both tasks must be written as full, connected text; notes and bullet points are penalised, and so is plagiarised (copied) text.
Write in an academic or semi-formal/neutral style.
There is no upper word limit. Writing more than the minimum is not penalised, but a long Task 1 costs time needed for Task 2.
Computer-delivered candidates type both answers, with a live word count on screen. Paper candidates write on the answer booklet.

task1.rubric_frame:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

{figure_sentence}

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
task1.closing_sentence: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
task_rules: An information-transfer task: describe only what the visual shows. Give no causes, speculation, recommendations or personal opinion beyond the data.
Select the key features (highest/lowest, biggest changes, main trends, exceptions) and support them with accurate figures and units; do not list every number.
A clear overview of the main trends, differences or stages is required for band 7+ (an attempted overview for band 6).
Paraphrase the prompt in the introduction; copied rubric is discounted.
Group information logically into paragraphs (commonly: introduction, overview, two body paragraphs).
Tense follows the data: past years → past simple; projections → future/predictive forms ('is expected to'); no time reference → present simple.
Tasks may combine two figures (e.g. a line graph and a pie chart, or a table and a bar chart); the overview then covers both and the body links them.

LINE.rubric:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

The graph below shows {description}.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
rubric_openers: The graph below shows …
The line graph below shows …
The graph below gives information about …
expected_structure: Introduction (1–2 sentences): paraphrase what is measured, the units, the categories/places and the time period.
Overview (2–3 sentences, few or no figures): the overall direction of each main line, the most striking change, which is highest/lowest over the period, and any crossover.
Body 1: detailed description of one group of lines (or the first part of the period), with figures at key points (start, peaks, troughs, end) and comparisons.
Body 2: the remaining lines (or the later period, including any projections), again with figures and comparisons.
No separate conclusion is needed; any final summary must restate the overview, not add opinion.
key_language: Upward: rise, increase, grow, climb, go up, surge, soar, rocket; a rise/increase/growth in …
Downward: fall, decline, decrease, drop, dip, plummet, slump; a fall/decline/drop in …
No change / variation: remain stable/steady/constant, level off, plateau, stabilise, fluctuate (around), show little change
Extremes: peak at, reach a high of, hit a low of, bottom out at, reach a peak of
Degree and speed: sharply, dramatically, significantly, considerably, steadily, gradually, moderately, slightly, marginally
Comparison: overtake, surpass, exceed, twice/three times as high as, the gap between X and Y widened/narrowed, in contrast, whereas, while
Approximation: approximately, roughly, around, just over/under, nearly, almost, well over
Time: over the period, between 1990 and 2010, from … to …, by 2020, in the following decade, thereafter, throughout the period
Projections: is projected/expected/predicted/forecast to rise; is likely to

BAR.rubric:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

The chart below shows {description}.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
rubric_openers: The chart below shows …
The bar chart below shows …
The bar chart below gives information about …
expected_structure: Introduction: paraphrase the measure, units, categories, groups and time(s).
Overview: the largest and smallest categories and the overall pattern; if the bars cover several years, the main trend(s) over time.
Body 1: compare one set of bars (e.g. the highest categories, or one group/year) with figures.
Body 2: compare the remaining categories or the other group/year, highlighting notable contrasts or exceptions.
Organise by comparison, not bar by bar in reading order.
key_language: Ranking: the highest/largest proportion, followed by, ranked second, the lowest figure was for …
Comparison: X was higher than Y, X was almost double Y, compared with, in comparison, by contrast, similarly, the same proportion as, respectively
Figures: the figure for X stood at …, X accounted for …, X reached …
Difference: exceeded by …, the difference between X and Y was …, significantly/slightly more than
Change over time (when years are shown): use LINE trend language

PIE.rubric:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

The pie charts below show {description}.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
rubric_openers: The pie chart below shows …
The pie charts below show …
The charts below give information about …
expected_structure: Introduction: paraphrase what the whole represents, the categories and the time(s) or places.
Overview: the dominant and smallest segments; for several pies, the main shifts in share between them.
Body 1: the largest segments (or the first pie) with percentages and comparisons.
Body 2: the smaller segments (or the second pie / the changes between pies).
Remember that pie charts show proportions of a whole: describe shares, not absolute amounts, unless totals are given.
key_language: Share: account for, make up, comprise, constitute, represent, form
Fractions and proportions: a quarter, a third, just under half, the majority, a minority, a small fraction, the remainder, the rest
Largest/smallest: the largest segment/share, the second largest, the smallest proportion
Change between pies: the share of X rose from … to …, X's proportion doubled/halved, X overtook Y as the main …
Accuracy: exactly, precisely, roughly, just over

TABLE.rubric:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

The table below gives information about {description}.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
rubric_openers: The table below shows …
The table below gives information about …
The table below compares …
expected_structure: Introduction: paraphrase the variables (rows and columns), units and time/place.
Overview: the most significant patterns: the highest and lowest items, general trends across columns, notable exceptions.
Body 1: one logical group (e.g. the top-ranked rows, or one variable) with selected figures.
Body 2: another group or variable, with contrasts.
Select and group; don't turn every cell into a sentence.
key_language: The figure for X was …, X stood at …, X recorded the highest …
Respectively (for paired figures), whereas, while, by contrast, in comparison
Ranking: ranked first, came second, the lowest was …
Proportion and multiples: twice as many, a third of, the vast majority
Trend language when columns are years

PROCESS.rubric:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

The diagram below shows {description}.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
rubric_openers: The diagram below shows the process by which …
The diagram below shows how … is produced/made.
The diagram below shows the stages in …
The diagram below shows the life cycle of …
expected_structure: Introduction: paraphrase what process is shown.
Overview: the number of stages, the start and end points, and whether it is a linear (manufacturing) or cyclical (natural) process.
Body 1: the first half of the stages in order, with the materials, equipment and conditions shown.
Body 2: the remaining stages to the end product (or back to the start of the cycle).
Mention every stage shown; describe it using the diagram's labels, but paraphrase them and build them into connected sentences.
key_language: Present simple passive: is harvested, is transported to, is crushed, is heated to, is filtered, is mixed with, is packaged, is delivered
Sequencers: first/initially/to begin with, at the first stage, next, then, subsequently, after that, following this, once X has been …, after which, before being …, finally, in the final stage
Purpose and result: in order to, so that, which results in, producing, to form
Cycle: the cycle then begins again, the process repeats
Active verbs for natural stages: the larvae hatch, the water evaporates, the eggs develop into …

MAP.rubric:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

The maps below show {description}.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
rubric_openers: The maps below show the changes to … between … and …
The maps below show … in … and the present day.
The plans below show …
The map below shows two possible sites for …
expected_structure: Introduction: paraphrase the place, time points (or proposed sites) and what is compared.
Overview: the overall nature of the change (e.g. more residential and modern, green space lost, transport improved), plus what stayed the same.
Body 1: changes in one area or of one type (e.g. buildings or housing), with locations.
Body 2: other changes (e.g. roads, facilities, green areas), with locations.
For two proposed sites: compare the sites' locations and features instead of changes over time.
key_language: Past passive for change: was demolished, was replaced by, was converted into, was extended, was expanded, was constructed/built, was relocated, was cleared, was added, was turned into
Unchanged: remained unchanged, was retained, still stands
Location: to the north/south-east of, in the north-west corner, adjacent to, next to, opposite, alongside, across from, on the site of, at the edge of, in the centre of, beside the river
Overall description: the area became more urbanised/developed, underwent significant redevelopment, was transformed
Plans or future: will be built, is to be converted, is planned to be

task2.opening_rubric:
You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.

Write about the following topic:
task_rules: The candidate must formulate and develop a position on a given prompt (a question or statement) about a topic of general interest suited to university entrants.
Answer every part of the question; the specific aspect asked, not the general topic.
Support ideas with explanation, evidence and examples (personal experience is allowed).
Four or five paragraphs is the conventional structure: introduction, 2–3 body paragraphs, conclusion.
Copied prompt language is discounted; paraphrase the statement in the introduction.

question_forms: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Do you agree or disagree?
To what extent do you agree or disagree with this opinion?
To what extent do you agree or disagree with this statement?
What is your opinion?
Is this a positive or negative development?
Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?
expected_structure: Introduction: paraphrase the statement and state a clear position (agree / disagree / partly agree, and to what extent).
Body 1: first main reason for the position, explained and supported with an example or consequence.
Body 2: second main reason; or, for partial agreement, the aspect the writer disagrees with, explained.
Optional body 3: acknowledge the opposing view and rebut it.
Conclusion: restate the position consistently and summarise the main reasons.
task_response_traps: Discussing both sides without ever committing to a position (TR ≤ 6 because the position/conclusions are unclear).
Changing position between the introduction and the conclusion.
'To what extent' means the degree of agreement must be clear; partial agreement is fine if explicit.

question_forms: Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
Discuss both views and give your opinion.
Discuss both these views and state your own opinion.
expected_structure: Introduction: paraphrase the two views and signal the writer's own opinion (or say it will be given).
Body 1: the first view, with reasons and an example, presented fairly.
Body 2: the second view, with reasons and an example; often the view the writer supports.
Conclusion: summarise both views and state the writer's own opinion clearly (it may favour one view or combine both).
task_response_traps: Omitting the writer's own opinion ('main parts incompletely addressed' → TR max 5).
Discussing only one of the two views in any depth.
Giving an opinion that contradicts the body paragraphs.

question_forms: What are the advantages and disadvantages of {X}?
Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?
Do the benefits of this outweigh the drawbacks?
Do the advantages of {X} outweigh the disadvantages?
expected_structure: Introduction: paraphrase the situation; for 'outweigh' prompts, state which side the writer considers greater.
Body 1: main advantages (1–2), explained with examples.
Body 2: main disadvantages (1–2), explained with examples.
Conclusion: summarise; for 'outweigh' prompts, confirm clearly which side is greater and why.
task_response_traps: For 'outweigh' prompts, listing pros and cons without weighing them (position unclear).
Discussing general advantages of a topic instead of the specific development in the prompt.

question_forms: What problems does this cause? What solutions can you suggest?
What problems might this cause? How could these problems be solved?
What are the causes of this problem? What measures could be taken to solve it?
What are the reasons for this? What can be done to solve this problem?
Why is this the case? What can be done about it?
expected_structure: Introduction: paraphrase the issue and preview problems/causes and solutions.
Body 1: 2 problems or causes, each explained with consequences or examples.
Body 2: solutions that clearly match the problems/causes given, with who should act and how.
Conclusion: summarise the main causes/problems and the most effective solutions.
task_response_traps: Writing about effects when causes are asked for (or the reverse).
Solutions that do not address the stated problems, or are vague ('the government should do something').
Spending almost all the words on one half of the question.

question_forms: Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?
What are the reasons for this? Is this a positive or negative trend?
Why do you think this is? What effects does this have on {X}?
Why is this the case? How could {X} be encouraged?
What are the reasons for this? What can be done to change it?
expected_structure: Introduction: paraphrase the situation and give a brief answer to both questions.
Body 1: a full answer to the first question (2 developed points).
Body 2: a full answer to the second question (with a clear view where it asks for an evaluation, e.g. positive or negative).
Conclusion: restate the answers to both questions.
task_response_traps: Answering one question fully and the other in a sentence (main parts incompletely addressed → TR max 5).
Treating the prompt as an agree/disagree essay instead of answering the questions asked.

task2.closing_rubric:
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
